tweets.title: Thrilled to share the news, officially released today, that I have been elected as a Fellow of The Royal Society of Canada | La Société royale du Canada (RSC),
tweets.body:
Thrilled to share the news, officially released today, that I have been elected as a Fellow of The Royal Society of Canada | La Société royale du Canada (RSC), class of 2026 – one of four foreign fellows across all fields of study, the annual limit set by RSC by-laws. From the RSC, “The Royal Society of Canada is Canada’s senior national academy. Founded in 1882, the RSC exists to promote Canadian research and scholarly achievement, recognize excellence, advise governments and organizations on matters of public interest, and foster the next generation of academic and creative leaders.”  https://t.co/wiNnZGuFdz
This recognition is particularly meaningful because of my many continuing professional ties to the science, engineering and medical communities in Canada – (1) We serve as the engineering team behind the Smart Hospital Project @SmartHospProj at Montreal Childrens Hospital, a program launched a few years ago and led by the chief neonatologist Dr. Guilherme Sant Anna @guisantanna  and his colleague Dr. Wissam Shalish and their team; (2) Several former postdoctoral members of the group are now faculty members at leading universities in Canada: Prof. Hyun-Joong Chung @ChungJoong  at the University of Alberta @University45322, Prof. Daniel Franklin at the University of Toronto @university28037, Prof. Shaghayegh Shajari at the Toronto Metropolitan University @TorontoMet and Prof. Yunyun Wu @Yunyun__Wu at Dalhousie, (3) Dr. Andrew Bonifas Ph.D., also a former postdoc, is Senior Director at Gilead Sciences @GileadSciences in Edmonton; and (4) We have had many productive scientific interactions with leading academics in Canada over the years: Profs. Dr. Jamal Deen, Leyla Soleymani @SoleymaniLab, Fabio Cicoira, Robert Kearney, Natalia Nikolova, @DavidJuncker, Simon Whyte, Matthias Görges @MatthiasGoerges and others, (5) I have delivered 28 invited talks at conferences and universities in Canada over the last ~20 years. Another notable connection is that my grandfather on my mother’s side was born in Manitoba – given recent changes in legal requirements, this means that I now qualify for Canadian citizenship, dual with the US, something that I plan to pursue in the near future! Very honored to join the RSC. Looking forward to making it all official at the induction ceremonies in Ottawa in November!

tweets.title: Exciting conference this week at ETH Zürich-- the Eurosensors 2026 meeting, where I had the pleasure of delivering a plenary talk on the first day, yesterday, c
tweets.body: Exciting conference this week at ETH Zürich-- the Eurosensors 2026 meeting, where I had the pleasure of delivering a plenary talk on the first day, yesterday, covering our exploratory and translational work on sensors of skin flux: microfluidics for eccrine sweat and modulated microclimates for skin gases. Many outstanding presentations from both academic researchers and industry representatives – I found the latter particularly refreshing, hearing about the commercialization process and the new technologies in the commercialization pipeline! The day concluded with a large dinner event at a restaurant on the lake – excellent turnout, more than 500 attendees, corresponding to almost a doubling compared to last year’s meeting. Excellent work by the organizers in making it happen - led by Prof. Andreas Güntner @andreasguentner, with his team: Profs. Andreas Hierlemann @AHierleman10797 , Christofer Hierold, J. Daniel Prades and Markus Graf! I’ve visited @ETH six times over the last dozen years, I serve in some volunteer advisory roles for the university, and former postdoctoral fellow Prof. Hedan Bai is now a highly successful junior faculty member there, also with another former postdoc Dr. Shuo Li in a top research position – such an incredible talent density at this place, overall, an absolutely elite environment for engineering research, one of the best in the world! Always enjoy my visits, this time including some sidebar meetings with Andreas’ group and tours of his labs – thanks again for hosting and for the invitation to deliver a talk at this meeting!!

tweets.title: Here in beautiful Antwerp today for a plenary talk at the meeting of the European Society For Biomaterials on the opening evening, celebrating the 50th annivers
tweets.body: Here in beautiful Antwerp today for a plenary talk at the meeting of the European Society For Biomaterials on the opening evening, celebrating the 50th anniversary or the society. In a presentation titled “Materials for Bioresorbable Electronics,” I focused on the essential materials science aspects of our research in this area, with examples at the device level in temporary pacemakers for use during recovery from a cardiac surgery and ultrasound-readable tags for sensing deep tissue homeostasis. Very pleased to visit this part of Belgium, having in past years traveled only to Leuven in 2022 and to Brussels in 2009, also for conferences, although two different ones. Great turnout (~1500) for a well-organized event today, held in an impressive location next to the iconic train station in the middle of the old part of the city. Excellent string quintet performing a range of classical pieces for the opening and closing of the evening session, followed by a reception. Thanks to Profs. @VVlierberghePBM, @LiesbetGeris and @veerlebloemen for the invitation to participate and to them and the rest of the organizing committee for their work on putting together an outstanding meeting. Very pleased to take part!

tweets.title: Best of luck to Dr. @HakYoung_Ahn as she transitions from our group to a research position in Korea, details to be announced later. During her time here as a po
tweets.body: Best of luck to Dr. @HakYoung_Ahn as she transitions from our group to a research position in Korea, details to be announced later. During her time here as a postdoctoral fellow, Hak Young was a key driving force in the development of various bioresorbable, wireless devices for electrotherapy – from stimulating damaged peripheral nerves for accelerated rates of neuroregeneration to temporary cardiac pacing for enhanced patient outcomes during a postoperative recovery period.  These projects leveraged her broad expertise in materials science, semiconductor physics, radio frequency engineering and biomedical device design – and it included numerous collaborators and co-authors here in the group and across the medical community in Chicago and Los Angeles! We wish her big-time success in the next steps of her career!

tweets.title: Very interesting symposium at the American Chemical Society meeting today here in Chicago, organized by Phil Floyd, Dhriti Nepal, Paul Blakemore, Lucas Beagle (
tweets.body: Very interesting symposium at the American Chemical Society meeting today here in Chicago, organized by Phil Floyd, Dhriti Nepal, Paul Blakemore, Lucas Beagle (organizer and presider) and Yoko Bian (panel moderator) – Wearable Sensors: Chemistry-Powered Technologies for Better Health, Fitness and Security. I was fortunate to join a lineup of outstanding invited speakers to present some of the latest work in this space. My talk, titled ‘Wearable Devices for Sensing Molecular Flux from the Surface of the Skin,’ emphasized our research on platforms for dynamic measurements of transcutaneous flux of water vapor, volatile organic compounds (including alcohol) and CO2, with applications in wound care and tracking of neonatal health – of course, with show/tell prototype devices of various types from our labs! Other speakers included those from industry, academia, government labs and the medical community – amazing talks by Corey Ungaro, AJ Aranyosi, Manu Jain, James Christensen and Jacqueline Klosek. A highly engaging panel discussion at the end of the symposium touched upon challenges and opportunities in the field, with an emphasis on topics in chemistry and materials science – for us, chemically specific gas sensors and colorimetric reagents for sweat biochemical sensing are high on the list! Thanks again to Lucas and the other organizers for bringing us together to discuss these important topics!

tweets.title: Pleased to announce this year’s winners of the Rogers/Huang Medal for Research Collaboration, awarded through the Hagler Institute at Texas A&M University. Quot
tweets.body: Pleased to announce this year’s winners of the Rogers/Huang Medal for Research Collaboration, awarded through the Hagler Institute at Texas A&M University. Quoting from the press release https://t.co/9VbeBb2ylP “Eleven researchers from Texas A&M University, Johns Hopkins University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill were named recipients of the second annual Rogers/Huang Medal for Research Collaboration, the Hagler Institute for Advanced Study announced today. Awarded annually, the Rogers/Huang Medal recognizes the best collaborative research paper authored by a team that includes a current or former Hagler Fellow or Distinguished Lecturer and a Texas A&M student among the co-authors. This year’s winning submission was “Non-Mendelian inheritance of DNA methylation patterns in mice.” As described in a paper in the journal Nature Medicine, the authors used advanced DNA sequencing technologies to simultaneously measure genetic variants and epigenetic modifications on individual DNA molecules, revealing that about 7% of epigenetic marks are inherited differently than predicted by classical Mendelian genetics. The study also identified unexpected inheritance patterns, including paramutation and emergent epigenetic traits, laying the foundation for integrating genetic and environmental contributions to disease risk and, potentially, reversing disease risk through epigenetic mechanisms. The recipients will receive a $10,000 monetary award allocated equally among all the authors. Each author will also receive a physical medal and an invitation to the 2027 Hagler Institute Gala, where they will be recognized.” Our team had a very tough time in selecting just one of many truly outstanding applicants! Congratulations to these researchers!

tweets.title: For an innovative piece of materials science and electrical engineering, take a look at our most recent paper in the area of bioelectronics, published today in
tweets.body: For an innovative piece of materials science and electrical engineering, take a look at our most recent paper in the area of bioelectronics, published today in the current issue of Nature Electronics – “A Wirelessly Powered, Light-Controlled, Bioresorbable Stimulation System With Programmable Polyphasic Waveforms.” https://t.co/zpmKA5zDiR. Here, we introduce a scheme in which light illumination serves as a mechanism for precisely shaping the temporal and spatial profiles of electrical stimulation delivered to targeted tissues by a battery-free, flexible implant. The work includes not only detailed studies of all of the aspects in engineering science but also elaborate examples in advanced forms of control of cardiac rhythms and respiratory patterns, via cardiac pacing and phrenic nerve stimulation, respectively. The key to device operation is in the combined use of small-scale coils for radio frequency power transfer and miniaturized bipolar junction transistors for optical modulation – all constructed in materials that support high-performance operation but are uniquely defined by their ability to dissolve naturally and harmlessly inside the body following stable operation over a clinically relevant timeframe for treatment of temporary patient conditions. The paper is the result, primarily, of the efforts of a remarkably talented pair of former postdoctoral fellows in the group – Prof. Jong Uk Kim (now on the faculty at @SKKUni1398) and Prof. Seung Gi Seo (now on the faculty at Kumoh National Institute of Technology) – also with essential contributions from Dr. Hongkai Wang and Dr. Eric Rytkin in medically relevant demonstrations. Of course, the various roles of the many other co-authors were also very important. Key senior investigators include Prof. @IEfimov  (cardiac), Prof. @ColinFranzMDphd  (phrenic), Prof. Sung Hun Jin (BJT processing) and Prof. ZHENQIANG MA (BJT physics). Thanks to everyone for the great collaboration! Also, thanks to Prof. @JunChenLab for writing a nice News and Views perspectives piece on our work, published alongside our paper in this issue of Nature Electronics! https://t.co/K4jRIWBLeT

tweets.title: Great news -- Dr. Jianlin Zhou, a postdoc in the group, has recently accepted a faculty position at Rutgers University in the Department of Electrical and Compu
tweets.body: Great news -- Dr. Jianlin Zhou, a postdoc in the group, has recently accepted a faculty position at Rutgers University in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, and is now departing to start his independent research career! Jianlin joined our team here at the Querrey Simpson Institute for Bioelectronics (QSIB) at Northwestern University about three years ago after finishing his PhD at Cornell University under the supervision of Prof. Edwin Han. There, he had an outstanding record, with several high-quality papers on devices and analysis approaches for non-contact RF imaging of internal body processes. During his time with us, he led some very challenging projects in filamentary vital signs monitoring probes, with integrated soft robotics actuators, for use during fetoscopic surgeries (published in Nature Biomedical Engineering), in similar probes for application in the neonatal intensive care unit (submitted) and in pacemaker-integrated frameworks for transcatheter aortic valve replacement surgeries (in final stages of preparation). His deep background in RF physics and circuit design also served as the basis for a number of collaborative projects in transient radios, breastmilk sensors and others. Jianlin has been a fantastic group member and he is certain to become a leader in electrical engineering research for medical systems, advanced communication networks and others – congratulations again your new position, and we look forward to many opportunities for continued interactions and future collaborations!

tweets.title: Our latest paper, published yesterday as the front cover feature article in the current issue of the journal Lab on A Chip, represents a contribution to an impo
tweets.body: Our latest paper, published yesterday as the front cover feature article in the current issue of the journal Lab on A Chip, represents a contribution to an important area of technology, which was completely new for us three years ago when we started – centrifugal microfluidics, in which a spinning disc with embedded microchannels, valves and reservoirs allows for complex chemical manipulations without external pumping apparatus. The work, titled “Centrifugal Microfluidics for Rapid Target Analyte Quantification in Airborne Bioaerosols,” represents a collaborative effort involving investigators and funding support at the Human Performance Wing of the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL), along with several other groups. Dr. Soongwon Cho, a former postdoctoral fellow now on the faculty at Kyung Hee University, was responsible for building the necessary technology in our labs, starting from scratch, in a very impressive and largely independent effort. The results demonstrate an ability for rapid on-site detection and identification of dangerous bioaerosols using a specialized sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, executed entirely in a complex centrifugal microfluidic platform of Soongwon’s customized design. We recently extended this technology to allow for related forms of chemical analysis of microliter volumes of sweat – to be announced in a separate post at a later time. Very much appreciate the broader team of researchers who contributed to this expansive effort – particularly Dr. Mike Brothers and Dr. Steve Kim, both of AFRL.

tweets.title: The final day for this trip Hong Kong and Jiaxing began with conference talks at the ICCES meeting and then a stimulating lunch with former group members and Pr
tweets.body: The final day for this trip Hong Kong and Jiaxing began with conference talks at the ICCES meeting and then a stimulating lunch with former group members and Prof. Yonggang Huang, talking about research, funding, grand challenges in bioelectronics, startup companies and others. Great to see everyone – Prof. Yang Chai, Prof. Jiaqi Liu, Prof. Xinge Yu, Prof. Jizhou Song, Prof. Zhaoqian Xie, Prof. Yihui Zhang, Prof. Xue Feng and Prof. Yuda ZHAO (academic grandson). The day wrapped up with a fireside chat, with Yonggang, and dinner event with members of the Northwestern University Club of Hong Kong – very impressive collection of individuals, all interested in processes for converting academic engineering innovations into commercial products. We talked not only about our own experiences but also about the infrastructure and mechanisms that have been put in place at Northwestern over the last several years, many enabled by the leadership of Lisa Dhar and the philanthropy of Kimberly Querrey. Very instructive to hear about similar, parallel activities in Hong Kong, guided by discussion with Prof. Michael Yang, the Yeung Kin Man Chair Professor of Biomedical Sciences, Senior Vice-President (Innovation and Enterprise) and head of City University of Hong Kong “HK Tech 300” initiative, the leading university-based entrepreneurship program in Asia. Helen Chen served as an excellent moderator! Thank you to Andrea Chen for reaching out and for help with all of the arrangements!

tweets.title: Second day at the ICCES meeting in Hong Kong kicked off with a series of truly amazing plenary presentations on the use of AI methods in computational modeling
tweets.body:
Second day at the ICCES meeting in Hong Kong kicked off with a series of truly amazing plenary presentations on the use of AI methods in computational modeling – from solid mechanics to thermal transport and fluid dynamics. The future is shaping up to be very exciting, completely transformative. The day concluded with a truly huge banquet event (~2000 people) with live, high-level performances of traditional Chinese dance and music, and with a series of award presentations – including a collection of medals: the Eric Reissner Medal to CT Lim, the J. N. Reddy Medal to Xu Guo, the Kobayashi Medal to Judith Driscoll, the Wei-zang Chien Medal to Yiu Wing Mai, the T. H. H. Pian Medal to Xue Feng, the John Rogers/Yonggang Huang Medal to George Pharr and Warren Oliver (deceased), capped by the two most prominent: the Satya N. Atluri Medal to Vikram Deshpande and the KC Hwang Lifetime Achievement Medal to me (and by extension to my collaborators). I was deeply honored by the opportunity to present, with Yonggang, the medal to George and, of course to receive the KC Hwang Medal. The citation for the latter is “For his pioneering contributions to the mechanics of soft electronic systems and for his role in establishing the field of bioelectronics, blending engineering science, biological research and medical practice.” Vikram and I were asked to make brief comments upon receiving our medals. Mine were as follows – “Tremendous honor, of course, to receive this recognition. I’d like to start by thanking the organizers for putting together a truly wonderful event - in particular, grateful to Prof Kun Zhou for all of his very hard work in making this happen.  I also appreciate the selection committee for thinking of me for this award.
Any award of this magnitude is a great honor, of course, but for me it’s also a recognition of the many amazing collaborators and students I’ve had over the years. Very interestingly, one of those collaborators is in fact the namesake for this award - the great, legendary mechanician Prof KC Hwang, with whom I co-authored 35 papers over a more than a decade period from 2008 to 2019, the last one coming just three years before his passing in 2022 at the age of 95. My connection to him also extends to his son, Prof. Yonggang Huang with whom I have published more than 400 papers over more than twenty years. So, I am deeply grateful, on behalf of these and many other of my collaborators and my current and former students, and I am humbled to accept this recognition - which has a very special meaning to me. Congratulations also to all of the other awardees for their impressive accomplishments. Thank you again.”

tweets.title: At the end of the first day of the ICCES conference: dinner with the ‘Royals’ – a collection of Fellows of the Royal Society: Prof. Norman Fleck, Prof. Chwee Te
tweets.body: At the end of the first day of the ICCES conference: dinner with the ‘Royals’ – a collection of Fellows of the Royal Society: Prof. Norman Fleck, Prof. Chwee Teck (C.T.) Lim, Prof. Yonggang Huang, Prof. Kun Zhou, Prof. Vikram Deshpande, Prof. Huajian Gao and his spouse Joan Gao. Wonderful conversations and excellent food, with an incredible view of Victoria Harbour, the surrounding city and drone light shows! Big thanks to Kun for organizing!

tweets.title: Finishing up the first day of a very powerful meeting – the 32nd International Conference on Computational and Experimental Engineering and Sciences (ICCES2026)
tweets.body: Finishing up the first day of a very powerful meeting – the 32nd International Conference on Computational and Experimental Engineering and Sciences (ICCES2026) here in Hong Kong. The speakers included, incredibly, an all-star lineup of 10 members of the US National Academy of Engineering (NAE), 9 Fellows of the Royal Society (FRS), 7 members of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), 3 members of the US National Academy of Engineering (NAS), 2 members of the Chinese Academy of Engineering (CAS) and 1 member of the National Academy of Medicine (NAM) – delivering talks in front of an audience of ~2000! I gave the second plenary talk in the morning – a tough job, as I had to follow immediately after the lead-off plenary by the great Prof. Norman Fleck. Because I am receiving the inaugural Keh-Chih Hwang Lifetime Achievement Medal at this meeting, I spent the first third of my talk, titled “Mechanics for Bioelectronics – and a tribute to K.-C. Hwang,” laying down a high-level summary of the amazing career of the great Prof. K.C. Hwang (1927-2022), featuring a few anecdotes from my interactions with him.  He has left behind a broad cohort of former group members who are now prominent members of the academic research community – several of whom are current collaborators. Perhaps his most important legacy, however, is in his son, Prof. Yonggang Huang – a close friend, a long-time co-author (>20 years, >400 papers, >100,000 citations), with a record of accomplishments that has earned him membership in the NAS, NAE, RS, CAS and others. The remainder (and much less important) of my talk focused on our work in soft and 3D electronics for interfaces to the human body and to human stem cell derived organoids, respectively. Deeply honored to be connected with Prof K.C. Hwang through this award, through 35 journal articles co-authored with him spanning 2008 to 2019, through collaborations with his former group members and through an academic partnership with his son. Touched to have the opportunity to deliver a tribute to the “Great Master of Rigor”, the “Mr. Big at Tsinghua University”, in front of this large, high-level academic audience. Thank you to Prof. Zuankai Wang, Prof. Li Shaofan, Prof. Jian Lu, Prof. Gang Wang and Prof. Kun Zhou as conference chairs for putting together a truly memorable event!

tweets.title: Talent overload! Amazing first day of talks here at the 7th Annual International Conference on Flexible Electronics. I was pleased to serve as one of three plen
tweets.body: Talent overload! Amazing first day of talks here at the 7th Annual International Conference on Flexible Electronics. I was pleased to serve as one of three plenary speakers, with Prof. George Malliaras and Prof. Jinsong Leng, to kick off the day this morning. My presentation was in two separate parts, one with a translational emphasis involving skin-interfaced wearable devices for chemical analysis of eccrine sweat (colorimetric microfluidics) and skin gases (dynamic microclimates), and the other on bioresorbable devices for electrotherapy (bioelectronic medicines). An incredible five parallel sessions followed throughout the afternoon, with excellent speakers in every one – extremely difficult to decide where to spend my time, I ended up jumping from one conference room to another, trying to take it all in. Selected highlights, among too many to mention here, included talks by Prof. Tae-il Kim, Prof. Martin Kaltenbrunner, Prof. Jae-Woong Jeong, Prof. Enming Song, Prof. Dae-Hyeong Kim, Prof. YongAn Huang, Prof. Li Zhang, Prof. Cunjiang Yu, Prof. Xing Sheng, Prof. Xinge Yu, Prof. Linqian Chang, Prof. Sihong Wang, Prof. Jun Chen – whew! Great to catch up with many of these speakers and other attendees, including a large number who are former group members – around 30 in total. The day concluded with a spectacular dinner event and live entertainment! Huge thanks to Prof. Xue Feng, Prof. Yihui Zhang, Prof. Heling Wang, Prof. Yonggang Huang and many others for making the event possible. Looking forward to day two tomorrow!

tweets.title: Congratulations to Dr. Taehoon Kim on his departure to a faculty position in Materials Engineering at a top 10 university in Korea (public announcement with det
tweets.body: Congratulations to Dr. Taehoon Kim on his departure to a faculty position in Materials Engineering at a top 10 university in Korea (public announcement with details will occur shortly) after successfully executing on some exciting research as a postdoctoral fellow in our group over the last year and a half! Taehoon came to us very highly recommended by Prof. Fiorenzo Omenetto at @TuftsUniversity where he was a PhD student. Fio is a good friend, and a co-author on nearly 25 papers over the last 15 years – starting with a @DARPA seedling project in 2008 that also involved his colleague, and another good friend, Prof. David Kaplan on a new concept: physically transient electronics - where our initial demonstrations involved silicon nanomaterials for the semiconductor and silk fibroin for the substrates and encapsulation layers. Foundational work that became the catalyst for a ~$100M investment by @DARPA to support a broad collection of efforts in this area. Taehoon brought this type of powerful mindset – new materials in support of new technologies -- to our group along with his deep domain knowledge in the materials science of silk.  He also quickly expanded his involvement into various other aspects of biomaterials and biosensing while here at @NorthwesternU, making major contributions along the way.  Specifically, he worked in a highly effective manner across projects ranging from transient nerve stimulators for pain block, to environmental monitors of hazardous substances, to platforms for monitoring volatile organic species from biological materials, including the skin. Several co-authored papers and a couple of manuscripts still in the works! Taehoon is an excellent scientist with a broad range of expertise, and we wish him all the best as he launches independent programs of research -- we look forward to on-going collaborative work as well as future opportunities!!

tweets.title: Cambridge NeuroWorks of the University of Cambridge and PAIR PolyU of the The Hong Kong Polytechnic University are two world-class institutions for academic res
tweets.body: Cambridge NeuroWorks of the University of Cambridge and PAIR PolyU of the The Hong Kong Polytechnic University are two world-class institutions for academic research, both with an orientation that includes an emphasis on translational efforts founded on scientific discoveries. The partnership between these two groups promises to unlock technologies of broad utility in neuroscience research and patient care. I was delighted to give an opening keynote talk this morning as part of a sponsored Joint Seminar and Webinar series. My talk was the second in this series, following a presentation last month by Prof. Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco – tough act to follow, but luckily with only modest overlap, given my own focus on engineering science and innovation. Titled ‘Bioelectronic Systems as Neural Interfaces,’ I provided an overview of work in this space, starting historically with one of our first papers, published in the journal Nature Materials in 2010 on ultrathin (micron and sub-micron), open mesh electronics for monitoring brain activity https://t.co/Cr57AOg2SP – a very common engineering theme in neural interfaces these days, across many groups, worldwide. Our ‘high-water’ marks in that general technology approach included active semiconductor nanomaterial-based systems with thousands and tens of thousands of channels published in Science Translational Medicine (2020) and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2019), respectively. The main part of my talk focused, however, on highly active areas of our current programs – microscale LEDs for control and monitoring of neural activity, and 3D mesoscale electronic frameworks as interfaces to cortical and spinal organoids. Thanks again to Prof. @GeorgeMalliaras  and Prof. Qingyan Chen for the invitation, and to Qingyan, Prof. Zijian Zheng and Prof. Sir John Aston for kind introductory comments – and to all of the other participants for their excellent presentations and discussions!

tweets.title: Very engaging visit of Toni Schrofner, Chief Officer of the Medical Division at Dräger, yesterday and today to our twin Querrey-Simpson Institutes (QSI) here at
tweets.body: Very engaging visit of Toni Schrofner, Chief Officer of the Medical Division at Dräger, yesterday and today to our twin Querrey-Simpson Institutes (QSI) here at Northwestern University: for Bioelectronics (QSIB; in Evanston) and for Translational Engineering for Advanced Medical Systems (QSI-TEAMS; in Chicago). Toni provided some excellent feedback on our work in wireless biomedical technologies for patient care, with powerful perspectives as the main representative of Drager’s partnership with Sibel Health, a spin-out company from our group. Thanks to the group members who presented and supported live demos, Dr. Min-Seung Jo, Dr. Jianlin Zhou, Jacob Trueb, Jay Kwak, Dr. Priscilla Fok, Monica Li, Ani Srinivasan, JK Chang (Wearifi Team), Dr. Xiao Xiao, Kiana Mohammadian and Amey Kasbe -- paired in each case with one or more of our clinical collaborators and their teams: Dr. Guilherme Sant'Anna and Dr. Wissam Shalish for NICU applications, Dr. Paul Cremer for cardiology, Dr. Ankit Bharat and Dr. Teja Devarakonda for pulmonology, Dr. Debra Weese-Mayer for NICU and Dr. Aimen Shaaban for NICU/PICU and fetal surgery. Thanks to everyone – and also especially to the great Anthony Banks -- for a collection of highly productive meetings and discussions on follow-up opportunities!

tweets.title: Thanks to Prof. Ravinder Dahiya for the invitation to give a presentation today (virtual) at the IEEE BENE (Beneficial Materials and Electronics) conference – f
tweets.body: Thanks to Prof. Ravinder Dahiya for the invitation to give a presentation today (virtual) at the IEEE BENE (Beneficial Materials and Electronics) conference – focusing on an area, physically transient electronics, that has been of interest to us since the ~2007/2008 timeframe when I initiated and led a study report on this topic during my service on the Defense Science Research Council to inform the Defense Advanced Projects Agency on new research opportunities of military relevance (i.e. ‘unrecoverable’ sensitive electronic technologies).  The core concepts culminated in our first paper, published in Applied Physics Letters back in 2009 (https://t.co/9OmKvULP08) and titled ‘“Silicon Electronics on Silk as a Path to Bioresorbable, Implantable Devices,” as a ‘partially’ bioresorbable technology – then soon followed with our ‘breakthrough’ observation that ultrathin, device-grade silicon is water soluble to benign end products, described in a paper, titled ‘“A Physically Transient Form of Silicon Electronics,” that appeared in Science in 2012 (https://t.co/MO79KmY9qj) as a fully bio/ecoresorbable approach (following a very long, arduous process with the referees – quite amusing in retrospect, extremely frustrating at the time…). Great to see the rapidly growing interest in this space – both for advanced medical implants to serve temporary needs and for reduced solid e-waste across all areas of consumer and industrial electronics! Implications spanning improved care of patients to sustainable care of our environment!

tweets.title: Skin stiffness can serve as a powerful clinical diagnostic indicator for a range of skin disorders. Our paper published today in the journal Science Advances re
tweets.body: Skin stiffness can serve as a powerful clinical diagnostic indicator for a range of skin disorders. Our paper published today in the journal Science Advances reports a small, wireless device with the ability to accurately and quickly measure stiffness at different depths into the skin and at different body locations (https://t.co/jntfYLfVqH). The mechanism relies on a small haptic actuator – like the ‘buzzer’ in your smartphone – to create vibrational motions in the skin, measured simultaneously with an integrated accelerometer. The magnitudes and frequencies of these motions define the stiffness when interpreted using rigorous theoretical models of the physics of this coupled mechanical system. This approach represents a convenient, compact and translatable scheme for soft tissue modulus determination, complementary to those reported in previous papers from our group (https://t.co/yyXWYryVv3 and https://t.co/1Y6wxTQvZP), focused on somewhat different use cases – and, of course, much more quantitative than basic manual palpation, currently the most widely used method. Clinical pilot studies reported in our paper include assessments of patients who suffer from lymphedema as well as those with scleroderma – information that can detect early signs, and track responses to medications and other therapies. The technology thus provides physicians with an important tool to guide decisions related to care of their patients – applicable in the hospital or the home. Congratulations to Dr. Min-Seung Jo (postdoc in the group), Prof. Hee Sup Shin (former postdoc) and Prof. @Jimmy_Mechanics  (former postdoc) for leading the engineering parts of this project, to Dr. Shupeng Li for the theoretical analysis, and to our main senior clinical collaborators Dr. Ann Marie Flores (lymphedema), Dr. Jodi L. Johnson (lymphedema), Dr. Fredrick Wigley (scleroderma) and Dr. Carrie Richardson (scleroderma), and their teams, for the patient interface, study coordination and medical perspectives. Big thanks also to our long-term collaborator Prof. Yonggang Huang for leadership on the theoretical aspects – and, of course, to all of the other co-authors for their important contributions! A short writeup with quotes from Dr. Jo and Dr. Flores can be found on our @NUFeinbergMed website, at https://t.co/Fa1OD7oDHh. Thanks to @MelissaLRohman for her efforts on this piece,

tweets.title: Wow!! What a mind-blowing level of intellectual power and academic research talent all in one place at the IEEE FLEPS meeting in Atlanta at Georgia Tech  – very
tweets.body: Wow!! What a mind-blowing level of intellectual power and academic research talent all in one place at the IEEE FLEPS meeting in Atlanta at Georgia Tech  – very prominently featuring a large collection of former group members (17 of them joined for drinks at the end of the first day, see pic) as invited speakers, panelists and session chairs, deeply honored to be affiliated with this group of high-quality people: Prof. @cunjiangyuUIUC, Prof. @yayun_du, Prof. Raudel Avila, Prof. Wei Ouyang, Dr. @SMadhvapathy , Prof. Amay Bandodkar, Prof. @PhilippGutruf , Prof. @NiLabDuke, Prof. @baiwubin, Prof. W. Hong Yeo, Prof. Dae-Hyeong Kim, Prof. Youn Joung Kang, Prof. SukWon Hwang, Prof. Jayhun Koo, Prof. @Luyao_Lu_GW, Prof. Ha Uk Chung, Prof. @ProfMattFlavin, Dr. @stevexuMD, Dr. @chad_webb and Dr. @roozyg. I was fortunate to give the opening keynote talk, titled ‘Flexible Electronics in 3D Functional Mesosystems: From Neural Interfaces to Environmental Monitors,’ pretty much self-explanatory on the content. Great event, excellent speakers and powerful science and technology throughout – I learned quite a bit through the talks and all of the other interactions! Big congratulations to the general co-chairs, Prof. W. Hong Yeo and Prof. @WeiGaoLab  and to the technical co-chairs Prof. @ProfMattFlavin and Prof. @locchipi for putting together an amazing program and overall event – and thanks also to the main IEEE Sensors Council representative, Prof. @RavinderSDahiya, for additional help and sponsorship. Looking forward to the rest of this meeting and to next year's meeting at @Cambridge_Uni!
